Chapter 3: Discovering the Real Jobs—Methods for Uncovering Customer Motivation
You know, figuring out the real job a customer wants to get done? It's rarely as simple as just asking them. Most people don’t talk about their needs in terms of progress or outcomes.
Instead, they’ll mention features they like, things that frustrate them, or compare your product to something else. The real trick is to dig deeper—to uncover what’s really driving their choices.
So, how do you do that? Well, one of the best ways is to study the context behind their decisions. That means watching customers in the wild—in real-life situations—having open-ended conversations, and piecing together the story that leads up to a purchase or a new habit. The aim is to really understand the customer’s struggle, and that pivotal moment when they decide to “hire” a solution.
There are some great techniques to help with this:
First, try what’s called a switch interview. Talk to people who’ve just started using a new product or service. Ask them what made them switch, what other options they looked at, and what finally got them over the line. This helps you see the actual job they needed done.
Another approach is to simply observe people in their own environment. Watch how they really use products—no scripts, no surveys. You’ll spot unspoken needs and clever workarounds that most folks would never mention in a questionnaire.
And don’t forget to map out the customer journey. Pay attention to the emotional highs and lows, the little obstacles that pop up, and the moments that bring satisfaction—or disappointment.
All of these methods come down to empathy and curiosity. You’ve got to leave your assumptions at the door and be open to being surprised. Sometimes, what looks like a desire for convenience turns out to be a need for control, or maybe just some extra reassurance.
Here’s a helpful way to picture what’s really happening: think of a tug-of-war. On one side, you’ve got the forces pulling someone toward a new solution—maybe they’re frustrated with what they have, or they see something new and promising. But on the other side, you’ve got the comfort of the familiar, the anxiety that comes with change, and the uncertainty about whether that new thing will actually work.
If you can map out these forces, you’ll spot the best levers for innovation. You can design products or services that make it easier for customers to move forward—while easing the worries that might hold them back. That way, your offering just feels like a natural fit, making the choice feel way less risky and a whole lot more rewarding.
Real-life stories really bring this to life. Take a mattress company, for example. They discovered that people put off buying a new mattress—not because they didn’t want one, but because shopping for one felt confusing and stressful. By simplifying the process and tackling delivery and setup worries head-on, they opened up a whole new wave of demand that was hidden before.
So, uncovering the real jobs customers need done? It’s a mix of art and science. You need sharp observation, thoughtful questions, and the guts to challenge what you think you know. When you do it well, you’ll find opportunities for innovation rooted in real life—not just in abstract data or wishful thinking.
